summary: This is a Science perspective by Melinda C. Mills (University of Oxford) on Ganna et al.'s large genome-wide association study of same-sex sexual behavior. The study used about 409,000 UK Biobank and 68,500 23andMe participants and found five loci, with small overall genetic effects. The piece stresses that genetics explains only a small share of behavior, that the findings cannot predict or alter orientation, and that the study's samples are limited in ancestry, age and socioeconomic diversity. The note also contains a fragment on tRF regulation of legume-rhizobium nodulation that appears to be from a different article, which is not digested here.
one_line: Perspective on Ganna et al.'s GWAS finding five genetic loci linked to same-sex sexual behavior, with small effects and no predictive use.
key_facts: Ganna et al. report the largest study to date on genetic variants associated with same-sex sexual behavior, comprising almost half a million individuals in the United Kingdom and United States.
Ganna et al. analyzed ever having sex with a same-sex partner using SNPs from the UK Biobank (408,995 individuals) and 23andMe (68,527 individuals from the United States).
Ganna et al. discovered five loci correlated with ever having same-sex behavior: two loci across both sexes, two in males, and one in females.
The average number of loci found in all GWASs from 2005 to 2018 is 13.6, according to the note.
The across-sex genetic correlation found by Ganna et al. was a weak 0.63.
Ganna et al. estimated that genetics could account for an upper limit of 8 to 25% of same-sex sexual behavior at the population level via SNP-heritability.
When all SNPs identified from the GWAS were combined into one score, they explained less than 1% of same-sex sexual behavior.
The genetic correlation for ever having same-sex sex versus proportion of same-sex partners was 0.73 for men and 0.52 for women.
Ganna et al. did not find evidence that sexual orientation is associated with variants on the X chromosome.
Male-specific loci were linked to olfactory receptor genes and to a variant upstream of the transcription factor 12 (TCF12) gene and a variant downstream of the sex-determining region Y (SRY) gene.
The study includes only European-ancestry populations from Western high-income countries, with 23andMe mean age 51.3 years and UK Biobank aged 40 to 69 years.
Same-sex orientation remains criminalized in more than 70 countries, some with the death penalty, according to the note.
Mills concludes that using these results for prediction, intervention, or a supposed cure is wholly and unreservedly impossible.
Mills calls for a multidisciplinary sociogenomic approach to study how genetic predispositions are altered by environmental factors.
